question: INR depreciates 83/$ to 88/$. Which company benefits MOST?
before: TCS earns ~95% revenue in foreign currencies, pays most costs in INR. Rupee weakening 83 to 88: each dollar converts to more rupees, boosting margins ~150-200 bps. IOCL hurt (pays more for oil). DLF neutral. Adani hurt (USD debt costlier).
after:
Concept: Currency depreciation affects companies differently based on their revenue and cost currency mix. When the rupee weakens (depreciates), companies earning foreign currency revenues gain a margin benefit when converting those revenues back to rupees, while companies with foreign currency costs face headwinds.

Step-by-step:
INR depreciates from 83/$ to 88/$. This means each USD earned now converts to 88 rupees instead of 83 rupees—a 6% weakening of the rupee. TCS earns approximately 95% of revenue in USD but incurs most operating costs in INR. When rupee weakens, the dollar earnings translate to more rupees at the same operational cost base, directly expanding net margins.

Result: TCS benefits most from this currency movement through margin accretion of approximately 150–200 basis points, while competitors face headwinds.

Why this is correct: TCS has the optimal currency mismatch for a depreciating rupee—high USD revenue (the stronger currency) paired with INR costs (the weaker currency). This is precisely the structural position that generates forex gains when the rupee weakens.

Why the others are wrong:

A) Indian Oil imports crude in USD, so rupee depreciation increases its input costs in rupee terms. A 6% rupee weakness means IOCL pays more rupees for the same dollar volume of crude imports, compressing rather than expanding margins.

B) DLF operates entirely in the domestic real estate market with revenues and costs both in INR. Currency movements do not materially affect its cash flows or margins since it has no foreign currency exposure.

D) Adani Enterprises carries USD-denominated debt. When the rupee weakens, the rupee value of that debt obligation rises, increasing interest expense and principal repayment burden in local currency terms—a direct headwind to profitability.

Intuition: Equity analysts screen for natural forex hedges when modeling earnings under currency regimes. A company with strong USD revenues and INR cost base acts as an unhedged long-dollar position, making rupee depreciation a tailwind to earnings. TCS's business model is a textbook case of this asymmetry, which explains why Indian IT services exporters historically outperform during rupee weakness cycles.
